Comparing student jobs? Include commuting time as well as travel costs. A higher advertised hourly rate can leave you with less money per hour of your day.
Ask whether a 6-hour shift includes an unpaid break. A 30-minute unpaid break means 5.5 paid hours, while the full 6 hours still uses your time.
A fictional $20/hour offer pays $440 for four 6-hour shifts with 30-minute unpaid breaks. With $32 travel costs and 6 commute hours, effective pay is $13.60/hour before tax.
Compare a typical week for each job. More weekly pay may mean more shifts, longer commutes or less time available for classes.
For a campus job with no travel charge, enter $0 travel costs. Keep any walking or commuting time in the comparison.
A nearby job can beat a higher hourly offer after travel. Compare gross pay, extra costs and the hours committed to each offer.
Before accepting a student job, ask: How long is each shift? Are breaks paid? How many shifts are usually available? Get the numbers first.
Count the round-trip commute, not just the trip to work. A 45-minute trip each way uses 90 minutes per shift.
For short shifts, commuting can take a large share of your day. Compare total time committed as well as hours on the clock.
Use extra work-related costs only. If you would buy the same lunch at home, the whole lunch price is not an extra cost of that job.
No unpaid break? Enter 0. A missing number and a genuine zero mean different things when comparing offers.
Benefits, learning opportunities and a good manager can matter more than small pay differences. Use the calculator for the money-and-time comparison, then consider those factors.
A fictional campus job at $16/hour for four 5-hour shifts with 10-minute round-trip commutes works out to about $15.48/hour of committed time before tax.
A weekly bus pass belongs in weekly work costs if it is an extra cost of taking the job. Do not also count that same pass per shift.
For driving costs, choose a consistent estimate across offers. Include parking and tolls when relevant, and avoid counting the same expense twice.
Write down the usual schedule before comparing offers. An advertised hourly rate does not tell you how many paid hours you will actually get.
Four 6-hour shifts commit 24 hours at work. If the breaks are unpaid, paid hours are lower. Keep those two measures separate.
When comparing a weekend job and an after-class job, consider both weekly income and committed hours. Each answers a different question.
Three job offers can look similar until you add travel costs. Put the same types of costs into each comparison so the numbers mean the same thing.
A fictional nearby cafe at $18/hour with four 6-hour shifts, 30-minute unpaid breaks, $2 travel per shift and 20-minute commutes comes to about $15.32/hour before tax.
Ask whether shifts are guaranteed or merely available. A comparison using four shifts will not match a week when you only receive two.
Effective pay in this calculator means pay after listed costs divided by all shift and commute hours. It is a comparison metric, not your payroll rate.
If a job needs paid equipment or a uniform, consider that extra cost. For a weekly comparison, use a realistic weekly share and explain your assumption.
Run the comparison again if your schedule changes. A longer shift can spread one round-trip commute over more paid hours.
A free parking spot reduces travel costs, but it does not remove the driving time. Money and time belong in separate inputs.
Keep tips and overtime out of a basic comparison unless you have a reliable estimate and a tool that models them. This workbook compares ordinary hourly pay.
For an unpaid break, subtract the break from paid time. Keep it inside shift time because you are still committing that part of the day to work.
The example offers show why the biggest hourly headline is not always the highest effective rate. The distant $20/hour job comes below the nearby $18/hour job.
Before you decide, compare a week with fewer shifts too. An uncertain schedule can change the weekly money you expect, even when the hourly rate stays the same.
Got a student job offer? Gather the hourly rate, usual shifts, shift length, unpaid breaks, round-trip commute and extra costs. Compare the week before accepting.
